question: Should I pick the high-deductible plan with an HSA or the PPO? I rarely see a doctor.

figures.label: HDHP yearly cost, low-use year (net of company HSA money)
HDHP yearly cost, high-use year (net of company HSA money)
Room left for your own HSA money (2026 self-only limit $4,400 minus company $500)
Tax saved by putting $3,900 in the HSA through payroll
figures.note: 22% federal bracket + 4.4% Colorado + 7.65% FICA (payroll HSA deductions skip FICA).

must_include: Yearly cost of each of the three plans in a low-use year: PPO 750 about $1,612, PPO 1500 about $988, HDHP about -$32 after the company's $500 HSA deposit.
Yearly cost of each plan in a high-use year that reaches the out-of-pocket max: PPO 750 about $5,112, PPO 1500 about $5,988, HDHP about $6,468.
For someone who rarely sees a doctor, the HDHP costs least; it costs most if the year goes badly, by about $1,356 versus the PPO 750.
The HSA tax benefit: money goes in before tax, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free for medical costs, and the account is yours if you leave.
Preventive care is free on all three plans, so 'rarely see a doctor' visits like an annual physical cost $0 on any plan.
Suggests keeping enough savings (or HSA balance) to cover the HDHP deductible ($3,400) in case of a bad year.
Notes the choice is locked until open enrollment in November unless there is a qualifying life event.
must_not_include: Counting the HSA company contribution on the PPO plans.
Telling the user they must pick a plan, without the advisor disclaimer.

assumptions: Low-use year: preventive care only, so $0 out of pocket on every plan.
High-use year: claims large enough to reach each plan's in-network out-of-pocket max.
HSA tax saving uses the 22% federal bracket from ex1-take-home and assumes contributions go through payroll.

sources.what: HSA self-only contribution limit $4,400 (includes employer money)

notes: Edge cases for this example are in eval/edge_cases.md (family tier, mid-year hire proration, HSA plus FSA conflict).
